content: An egg yolk is the portion of an egg that functions as the primary nutritional source for the developing embryo within. Before fertilization, the yolk, along with the germinal disc, constitutes a single cell. In mammals, embryos rely on their yolk for sustenance until they implant into the uterine wall. The yolk is suspended in the egg white (formally referred to as albumen or ovalbumin) by one or two spiral bands of tissue known as chalazae. As a food source, egg yolks are rich in vitamins and minerals. They contain all of the egg's fat and cholesterol, as well as nearly half of its protein content. When left intact during cooking, such as in fried eggs, the yellow yolk surrounded by a flat layer of egg white creates the characteristic sunny-side up appearance. When the yolk and white are mixed before cooking, as in omelets or scrambled eggs, the result is a pale yellow dish. Uses of Egg Yolk Egg yolks are often separated from the egg white and used in culinary applications, such as in mayonnaise, custards, hollandaise sauce, crème brûlée, avgolemono, and ovos-moles. In traditional art, egg yolk is a key component of egg tempera, a type of paint. In microbiology, egg yolk is used to produce egg-yolk agar plate medium, which is instrumental in detecting Clostridium perfringens. Egg yolk contains an antibody called immunoglobulin yolk (IgY), which is transferred from the laying hen to the yolk, providing passive immunity to protect the embryo and hatchling from microbial infections. Egg yolk is also used in the production of certain liqueurs, such as Advocaat. Composition of Chicken Egg Yolk The yolk constitutes approximately 33% of the liquid weight of an egg and contains about 60 calories, which is three times the caloric content of the egg white. It is a rich source of fat-soluble vitamins, including vitamins A, D, E, and K. Notably, egg yolks are one of the few natural food sources of vitamin D. The fatty acid composition of egg yolk by weight is as follows: Unsaturated fatty acids: Oleic acid: 47% Linoleic acid: 16% Palmitoleic acid: 5% Linolenic acid: 2% Saturated fatty acids: Palmitic acid: 23% Stearic acid: 4% Myristic acid: 1% Egg yolk is also a source of lecithin, an emulsifier. A large yolk contains more than two-thirds of the recommended daily cholesterol limit of 300 mg, which is considered significant. The yellow coloration of the yolk is due to the presence of lutein and zeaxanthin, which are carotenoids classified as xanthophylls. Double Egg Yolks Double-yolked eggs occur when ovulation happens too quickly, or when one yolk becomes lost and is joined by the next yolk. These eggs are often produced by pullets (young hens) whose reproductive cycles are not yet fully synchronized. They may also be laid by heavy-breed hens, and the trait can sometimes be inherited. No-Yolk Eggs Eggs without yolks are referred to as dwarf or wind eggs. These are typically the result of a pullet's first attempt at laying, before her reproductive system is fully functional. In mature hens, wind eggs are rare but can occur if a small piece of reproductive tissue breaks away, triggering the egg-producing glands to treat it as a yolk. This tissue is then encased in albumen, membranes, and a shell as it moves through the oviduct. Such eggs can be identified by the presence of a small grayish tissue particle instead of a yolk. Historically, no-yolk eggs were called cock eggs because they were believed to be laid by roosters, as they cannot hatch. These eggs are found in various bird species, including chickens (both standard and bantam breeds), guinea fowl, and Coturnix quail.
